summary: For ages 9-11, this topic builds the idea that insect communication is a SIGNAL carrying INFORMATION that changes another insect's behaviour, without words. The star example is the honeybee waggle dance, which encodes two variables at once: the angle of the straight 'waggle run' gives direction (on the vertical comb in the dark hive, the run's angle from straight up stands for the flowers' angle from the sun's direction), and the duration of the waggle run gives distance. Supporting examples include ant pheromone trails (chemical messages that build up with traffic and fade unless reinforced), firefly flash patterns (species-specific codes), and cricket chirps. The monarch butterfly migration adds scale and navigation across generations, and is deliberately used as a contrast — remarkable behaviour that is NOT communication. Children should both DECODE and PRODUCE signals so the code is understood from both ends. Avoid over-anthropomorphising: insects signal, they do not 'talk' with words or conscious intent.
misconceptions: 'Bees talk / have a language like ours' — they signal information, without words or conscious intent.
'The waggle dance only shows direction' — it encodes distance too (via duration).
'Ant trails are permanent roads' — they are chemical signals that evaporate unless reinforced.
'All fireflies flash the same' — patterns are species-specific codes.
'One butterfly makes the whole migration round-trip' — the monarch migration spans multiple generations.

activities.title: Decode and perform the waggle dance
steps: Watch a forager bee perform a waggle dance: a straight 'waggle run' tilted at an angle, then a loop back, repeated over and over.

Read the two pieces of information: use the ANGLE of the straight run from straight up on the comb to work out the direction to the flowers (that same angle measured from the sun's direction), and use how LONG each waggle run lasts to judge the distance.
Set your heading at the dance's angle measured from the sun's direction and set a distance from the waggle duration, then 'fly out' to try to reach the flower patch.
If you overshoot, fall short, or head the wrong way, watch the bee dance again and adjust your reading.
Then swap roles: given a flower patch in a chosen position, perform the correct dance (right angle, right waggle length) so hive-mates could find it.
activities.insight: The little dance is a real message that carries TWO pieces of information at once — which direction and how far — a decodable code, not just excited wiggling. Producing the dance as well as reading it shows the code works from both ends.

activities.title: Lay an ant trail that strengthens and fades
steps: Draw a scent (pheromone) trail between the nest and a food source.
Watch what happens as more ants travel the trail — notice it strengthens with traffic.
Stop the traffic and observe the trail fade over time.
Explain in your own words why a trail is NOT a permanent road and what information it carries to other ants.
activities.insight: A pheromone trail is a chemical message: it carries 'food this way', builds up when reinforced by traffic, and evaporates when not — so it is a signal, not a fixed path.

activities.title: Match firefly flash patterns to species
steps: Observe different firefly flash patterns (timing and sequence of flashes).
Reproduce a given species' flash pattern.
Match a flash pattern to the species that uses it, and explain who the signal is for and why (finding a mate).
activities.insight: Flashes are species-specific codes — a signal using light. Different species use different patterns, so the pattern itself carries meaning to the right receiver.

activities.title: Navigate the monarch migration — and ask: is this communication?
steps: Trace the monarch butterfly migration across a continent-spanning map, following the route over thousands of kilometres.
Describe what makes the journey remarkable in terms of distance and navigation.
Note that the full round-trip spans multiple generations — one butterfly does not complete it alone.
Decide and justify: is migrating the same as communicating, or is it something different?
activities.insight: Migration is a remarkable navigational behaviour, but it is NOT communication — it does not pass information to another insect to change its behaviour. This contrast sharpens the definition of communication.

activities.title: Explain what the waggle dance does (diagnostic discussion)
steps: Consider the claim: 'When a honeybee finds flowers, it just gets excited and wiggles about.' Decide whether that is right.
Explain what the waggle dance actually does, what information it carries, and why that counts as communication.
Answer a follow-up: HOW does one dance show BOTH direction AND distance — what part of the dance carries each?
Explain whether an ant's chemical trail and a firefly's flash also count as communication, and why.
activities.insight: Communication is a signal that carries information and changes another animal's behaviour. The dance is not mere excitement: the angle encodes direction and the waggle duration encodes distance, and hive-mates decode it inside the hive before flying out on their own.

checkQuestion: When a honeybee finds a good patch of flowers, it goes back to the hive and does a 'waggle dance'. A child says: 'The bee is just excited and wiggling about.' Is that right? Tell me what the waggle dance actually does, what information it carries, and why that counts as communication.
checkAnswer: It's not just excitement — the waggle dance is communication. Through the direction and length of the waggle, the bee tells its hive-mates WHERE the flowers are: the angle of the dance shows the direction (relative to the sun) and the length/duration of the waggle shows the distance. Other bees read this and fly to the food. It counts as communication because one bee is deliberately passing useful information that changes what the other bees do — even though there are no words.
